steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Researching artists means understanding their CONTEXT — when, where and why they worked, not just what they made.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Critical analysis involves describing, analysing, interpreting and evaluating — move beyond I like it because it looks nice.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Key movements: Renaissance (realism, perspective), Impressionism (light, colour), Cubism (multiple viewpoints), Surrealism (dreams, subconscious), Abstract Expressionism (gesture, emotion), Pop Art (popular culture).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Your artist research should DIRECTLY inform your own work — do not just copy, respond and develop ideas.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Create a series of experimental studies exploring artists and art movements. Annotate your process. | Research an artist or designer who works with artists and art movements. Write a critical analysis of their approach and explain how it has informed your own work. | Evaluate the effectiveness of your experiments with artists and art movements. Which approaches were most successful and why?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: A range of experimental studies showing different approaches to artists and art movements, each annotated with media, technique and purpose. Show development from initial experiments to refined outcom | A critical analysis naming a specific artist/designer, using specialist vocabulary, explaining their context and approach, and making clear connections to personal work. | A reflective evaluation identifying successful and less successful experiments, explaining WHY using technical and conceptual language, and showing how evaluation led to further refinement.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Address ALL four Assessment Objectives — AO1 (develop), AO2 (refine), AO3 (record), AO4 (present) Show the FULL creative journey — from initial research to final outcome Annotate your work using specialist vocabulary (not just "I like it") Draw from primary sources wherever possible — real objects, not photos Experiment with a RANGE of media and techniques before selecting Make clear connections between artist research and your own developing work
